Why was Europe close to its financial tether by the time the United States entered the war?

Europe had run out of ordinary financial room to manoeuvre: it had already liquidated the private American assets its citizens held, and it could no longer buy arms for cash or pledge adequate collateral to borrow more.

Hudson's summary of the situation is direct:

> "That represented Europe's financial limit in terms of normal commercial standards. The continent was close to the end of its financial tether by the time the United States entered the war. It lacked means to purchase American arms for cash in the amounts required, and lacked adequate collateral on which to borrow further sums through U.S. banks." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 1, "Origins of Inter-Governmental Debt, 1917–1921")

The mechanism that got Europe to that point was the winding-down of its overseas investments:

> "private international claims were being wound back to American residents nearly $4 billion of U.S. railroad bonds, down by European governments requisitioning and reselling their common stocks and other securities. The result was a $7.5 billion shift in America's net investment position." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 1)

So European governments paid for munitions and supplies by commandeering and selling off their citizens' holdings of American railroad bonds, common stocks and other securities — a one-time liquidation of assets rather than a sustainable source of funds. Once that was spent, the only remaining channel was inter-governmental credit, and the debts piled up accordingly:

> "obligations of the Allies to the United States Government grew to $12 billion by 1921, starting with the above-mentioned $3 billion credit granted in 1917." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 1)

Context: this is Hudson's framing of how World War I transformed the United States from a net debtor into a net creditor and replaced private lending with government-to-government war debt — the "inter-governmental debt" of his chapter title.

The two bodies of evidence stage the same vocabulary — justice, liberty, rights — at very different scales, and with different confidence about whether full justice is achievable.

**Radical political activism: rights as collective and constitutional, aimed at power.** In Aptheker's account, English radicals treated American grievances as inseparable from English liberties: London's petition to the King held that "the liberties of the whole [Empire are] inevitably connected with those of every part," and that the ministers' measures sought "to establish arbitrary power over all America" (Aptheker American Revolution · England and the Revolution). The grievances were framed publicly, against Crown corruption: "Your petitioners are persuaded that these measures originate in the secret advice of men who are enemies, to your Majesty's title, and to the liberties of your people" (Aptheker American Revolution · England and the Revolution). The evidence suggests that leaving old ways can gain survival, unity, healing, and just judgment, while clinging to them can cost the larger good even when it preserves custom.

> “I was wrong,” he said. “The Harkonnens are not there. The war is not there.” (Dune · Chapter 43)

How does this commentary link the state to the imperialist war and the growing world proletarian revolution?

The link is causal and dialectical: the war drives state–capital fusion, that fusion intensifies oppression, oppression fuels the revolution, and the revolution turns the "question of the state" into a practical problem.

**1. War fuses the state with capital.** Lenin opens by noting that "The imperialist war has immensely accelerated and intensified the process of transformation of monopoly capitalism into state-monopoly capitalism" (State and Revolution · Preface to the First Edition). The result is "The monstrous oppression of the working people by the state, which is merging more and more with the all-powerful capitalist associations," such that "The advanced countries — we mean their hinterland — are becoming military convict prisons for the workers" (same chapter).

**2. That oppression matures the revolution.** "The unprecedented horrors and miseries of the protracted war are making the people's position unbearable and increasing their anger. The world proletarian revolution is clearly maturing. The question of its relation to the state is acquiring practical importance" (same chapter). So the state is not a neutral bystander in the war; it is the instrument through which war becomes class oppression, and that is precisely what produces revolutionary anger.

**3. The state thus becomes the central strategic question.** The revolution "as a whole can only be understood as a link in a chain of socialist proletarian revolutions being caused by the imperialist war," and so "The question of the relation of the socialist proletarian revolution to the state... is acquiring not only practical political importance, but also the significance of a most urgent problem of the day" (same chapter).

**4. And the obstacle is opportunist theory of the state.** Freeing workers from the bourgeoisie "is impossible without a struggle against opportunist prejudices concerning the 'state'"; hence Lenin's plan to examine "the theory of Marx and Engels of the state," the distortions of Kautsky and the Second International, and finally "the main results of the experience of the Russian revolutions of 1905 and particularly of 1917" (same chapter).

In short: imperialist war → state-monopoly capitalism → intensified state oppression → maturing world proletarian revolution → the state as the decisive theoretical and practical question. All of this is library-based from the Preface; the surrounding argument (that the revolution must smash, not inherit, the bourgeois state machine) is developed later in the work and is not stated in this excerpt.
